title: The Global AI Bust
gist: Ruchir Sharma opens by arguing AI is spreading faster than any innovation since the Industrial Revolution, but that past general-purpose technologies only delivered full economic payoffs decades later after complementary infrastructure was built. Only the opening is available (paywall); the title signals a bust thesis.

themes.theme: AI adoption versus historical technology lag

insights.claim: AI is spreading faster and more widely than any innovation since the dawn of the Industrial Revolution, by many measures.
insights.speaker: Ruchir Sharma
insights.so_what: Adoption speed is not in dispute, so the debate shifts to when and whether returns arrive.

insights.claim: Past transformative technologies did not deliver their full potential until complementary infrastructure was completed decades later: steam engines needed railways, electricity needed power grids, and business computers gave no visible economic lift before the Internet connected them in the 1990s.
insights.speaker: Ruchir Sharma
insights.so_what: Suggests a long gap between AI investment and measurable productivity gains, a risk for investors pricing near-term returns.

insights.claim: The article's framing, 'The Global AI Bust: What Will Survive When the Boom Ends', implies the author expects an AI boom to end in a bust.
insights.speaker: Ruchir Sharma
insights.so_what: A bust-then-survivors framing points to screening for AI winners that persist after the boom unwinds.
